questions.q: Which cellular adaptation is characterized by an increase in the size of individual cells resulting in an enlargement of the organ without an increase in cell number?
questions.explain: Hypertrophy involves an increase in cell size due to increased synthesis of structural proteins and organelles, typically seen in permanent cells like cardiac and skeletal muscle. Hyperplasia refers to an increase in cell number.

open.q: Name the cellular adaptation characterized by an increase in the size of individual cells resulting in organ enlargement without an increase in cell number.

questions.q: Which reversible change involves the replacement of one differentiated adult cell type by another differentiated adult cell type better suited to withstand an adverse environment?
questions.explain: Metaplasia is a reversible reprogramming of stem cells to differentiate along a new pathway in response to chronic irritation, such as squamous metaplasia in the respiratory tract of habitual smokers. Anaplasia is lack of differentiation seen in malignant tumours.

open.q: Name the reversible cellular adaptation in which one differentiated adult cell type is replaced by another differentiated adult cell type.

questions.q: Which intracellular pigment accumulates within cells undergoing brown atrophy of the heart and liver as a byproduct of free radical-induced lipid peroxidation?
questions.explain: Lipofuscin is an insoluble wear-and-tear pigment composed of polymers of lipids and phospholipids complexed with protein, imparting a brownish discoloration to atrophic organs in elderly or malnourished patients. Haemosiderin is an iron-storage pigment.

open.q: Name the intracellular wear-and-tear pigment that accumulates in cells undergoing brown atrophy of the heart and liver.

questions.q: A 52-year-old man with a 15-year history of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease undergoes upper endoscopy showing salmon-pink mucosa extending above the gastro-oesophageal junction. Biopsy shows intestinal-type goblet cells. What is the primary mechanism underlying this adaptation?
options: Proliferation of mature squamous epithelial cells
Reprogramming of local mucosal stem cells
questions.explain: Barrett oesophagus is an example of columnar metaplasia driven by cytokine and growth factor signals that reprogram undifferentiated mucosal stem cells to differentiate into gastric or intestinal epithelium. Mature differentiated cells do not directly convert into another mature type.

open.q: What is the primary cellular mechanism by which chronic acid reflux induces Barrett oesophagus in the distal oesophagus?

questions.q: Which intracellular degradation pathway is predominantly upregulated during nutrient deprivation and cellular atrophy to digest the cell's own organelles?
questions.explain: Autophagy involves sequestering intracellular organelles within double-membraned autophagosomes that fuse with lysosomes to recycle nutrients and reduce cell size during atrophy. Phagocytosis engulfs extracellular particles.

open.q: Name the intracellular lysosomal degradation pathway upregulated during starvation and cellular atrophy to digest a cell's own organelles.

questions.q: What is the earliest ultrastructural and light microscopic manifestation of almost all forms of acute reversible cell injury?
questions.explain: Cellular swelling (hydropic change) occurs first when ATP depletion causes failure of the plasma membrane sodium-potassium pump, leading to intracellular sodium and water accumulation. Karyorrhexis is a nuclear sign of irreversible cell death.

open.q: What is the earliest morphological manifestation of almost all forms of acute reversible cell injury?

questions.q: During acute hypoxic cell injury, a rapid fall in intracellular pH leads to clumping of nuclear chromatin. Which metabolic shift is directly responsible for this intracellular acidosis?
options: Stimulation of anaerobic glycolysis with lactic acid accumulation
Upregulation of the hexose monophosphate shunt
questions.explain: Hypoxia halts mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and reduces ATP, which stimulates phosphofructokinase and anaerobic glycolysis; glycogen is rapidly depleted and lactic acid accumulates, lowering intracellular pH.

open.q: Which metabolic pathway is stimulated during acute hypoxic cell injury to cause lactic acid accumulation and a fall in intracellular pH?

questions.q: Which plasma membrane pump fails first during ATP depletion, causing intracellular accumulation of sodium and water?
questions.explain: Loss of ATP impairs the energy-dependent Na+/K+-ATPase pump in the plasma membrane, causing sodium to enter and potassium to exit the cell along their concentration gradients, followed by isosmotic water influx.

open.q: Name the energy-dependent plasma membrane ion pump whose failure during ATP depletion leads directly to intracellular sodium and water accumulation.

questions.q: Detachment of ribosomes from the rough endoplasmic reticulum during reversible cell injury directly causes a reduction in which cellular process?
questions.explain: ATP depletion leads to detachment of ribosomes from the rough endoplasmic reticulum and dissociation of polysomes into monosomes, directly impairing cellular protein synthesis.

open.q: Which cellular biosynthetic process is directly impaired when ribosomes detach from the rough endoplasmic reticulum during reversible cell injury?

questions.q: Which intracellular ion acts as a crucial second messenger that activates phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases, and ATPases when its cytosolic concentration rises uncontrollably during cell injury?
questions.explain: Cytosolic free calcium is normally kept very low by sequestration in mitochondria and the endoplasmic reticulum; influx of extracellular calcium or release from intracellular stores activates destructive enzymes that damage membranes, cytoskeleton, and chromatin.

open.q: Name the intracellular ion whose uncontrolled cytosolic elevation during cell injury activates destructive phospholipases, proteases, and endonucleases.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the conversion of hydrogen peroxide into water and molecular oxygen within peroxisomes to protect cells from oxidative stress?
questions.explain: Catalase, located in peroxisomes, decomposes hydrogen peroxide into oxygen and water. Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide anions into hydrogen peroxide, whereas myeloperoxidase generates hypochlorous acid in neutrophils.

open.q: Name the peroxisomal antioxidant enzyme that decomposes hydrogen peroxide into water and molecular oxygen.

questions.q: In the presence of ferrous iron, hydrogen peroxide is converted into the highly reactive hydroxyl radical. What is the name of this chemical reaction?
questions.explain: In the Fenton reaction, ferrous iron (Fe2+) donates an electron to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) to generate ferric iron (Fe3+), a hydroxide ion, and the highly destructive hydroxyl radical (OH•) that initiates lipid peroxidation.

open.q: Name the iron-catalyzed chemical reaction in which ferrous iron converts hydrogen peroxide into the highly reactive hydroxyl radical.

questions.q: Which mitochondrial membrane channel opens irreversibly during severe cell injury, dissipating the proton gradient and halting ATP synthesis?
questions.explain: Opening of the high-conductance mitochondrial permeability transition pore (MPTP) in the inner mitochondrial membrane abolishes the mitochondrial membrane potential, prevents oxidative phosphorylation, and releases pro-apoptotic proteins like cytochrome c.

open.q: Name the high-conductance channel in the inner mitochondrial membrane whose irreversible opening dissipates the proton gradient and halts ATP synthesis.

questions.q: A 24-year-old man ingests a toxic dose of paracetamol. Hepatic centrilobular necrosis develops because cytochrome P450 converts paracetamol into NAPQI, which depletes which endogenous hepatocyte antioxidant?
questions.explain: N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) is normally detoxified by conjugation with reduced glutathione (GSH); once hepatic GSH stores are depleted, NAPQI covalently binds cellular proteins and causes free radical-mediated centrilobular necrosis.

open.q: Name the endogenous hepatocyte tripeptide antioxidant depleted by the toxic paracetamol metabolite NAPQI.

questions.q: A 58-year-old man undergoes successful percutaneous coronary intervention 90 minutes after occlusion of his left anterior descending artery, but develops ventricular arrhythmias and worsened myocardial enzyme release immediately after blood flow returns. Which mechanism best explains this additional myocardial damage?
options: Burst of reactive oxygen species and neutrophil recruitment upon reoxygenation
Abrupt inhibition of anaerobic glycolysis by insulin
questions.explain: Ischaemia-reperfusion injury occurs when restoration of blood flow to ischaemic tissue generates a surge of reactive oxygen species from damaged mitochondria and endothelial xanthine oxidase, alongside complement activation and neutrophil infiltration.

open.q: What pathological phenomenon explains paradoxical worsening of tissue injury immediately after restoration of blood flow to ischaemic myocardium?

questions.q: Which nuclear change in necrotic cells is characterized by fragmentation of the pyknotic nucleus into small basophilic particles?
questions.explain: Karyorrhexis is the fragmentation of a condensed (pyknotic) nucleus into scattered chromatin clumps. Pyknosis is nuclear shrinkage with increased basophilia, while karyolysis is fading of chromatin basophilia due to DNase activity.

open.q: Name the nuclear change during necrosis characterized by fragmentation of a shrunken nucleus into small basophilic particles.

questions.q: Which pattern of necrosis preserves the basic structural outline of dead cells and tissue architecture for several days due to denaturation of structural proteins and enzymes?
questions.explain: Coagulative necrosis is characteristic of ischaemic infarction in solid organs (except the brain), where acidosis denatures both structural proteins and lysosomal enzymes, blocking proteolysis and preserving cellular ghosts.

open.q: Name the pattern of necrosis in which cellular and tissue architectural outlines are preserved for days due to protein and enzyme denaturation.

questions.q: Ischaemic infarction of the brain characteristically results in which morphological type of necrosis?
questions.explain: Hypoxic death of cells within the central nervous system evokes liquefactive necrosis rather than coagulative necrosis, resulting in enzymatic digestion of brain tissue into a viscous liquid mass.

open.q: Which morphological pattern of necrosis characteristically occurs after ischaemic infarction of the brain?

questions.q: A 34-year-old Nigerian man presents with chronic cough, night sweats, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Excisional lymph node biopsy reveals amorphous, eosinophilic, cheese-like acellular debris surrounded by epithelioid macrophages and Langhans giant cells. What type of necrosis is present?
questions.explain: Caseous necrosis is most often encountered in foci of tuberculous infection (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), where tissue architecture is completely obliterated into a friable, yellow-white, cheese-like debris within a granuloma.

open.q: Name the distinctive pattern of necrosis characterized by cheese-like acellular debris within tuberculous granulomas.

questions.q: During acute pancreatitis, activated pancreatic lipases split triglycerides into free fatty acids that combine with calcium ions to produce chalky-white macroscopic deposits. What is the name of this chemical process?
questions.explain: In enzymatic fat necrosis, released free fatty acids bind calcium ions to form insoluble calcium soaps (saponification), appearing grossly as chalky-white areas in peripancreatic fat.

open.q: Name the chemical process in enzymatic fat necrosis where free fatty acids combine with calcium ions to form chalky-white calcium soaps.

questions.q: Which pattern of necrosis is typically seen in immune-mediated vasculitis and malignant hypertension, characterized by brightly eosinophilic, smudge-like proteinaceous deposits in arterial walls?
questions.explain: Fibrinoid necrosis occurs when immune complexes together with fibrin leaking out of damaged vessels deposit in arterial walls, producing a bright pink, amorphous appearance resembling fibrin on H&E staining.

open.q: Name the pattern of vascular wall necrosis characterized by brightly eosinophilic deposits of immune complexes and leaked plasma fibrin.

questions.q: Which intracellular enzyme family serves as the primary executioner of apoptosis by cleaving cytoskeletal and nuclear matrix proteins after aspartate residues?
questions.explain: Caspases (cysteine-aspartic proteases) exist as inactive zymogens that are activated in an initiator-to-executioner cascade (e.g., caspase-3 and caspase-7) to dismantle the cell cleanly during apoptosis.

open.q: Name the family of cysteine proteases that act as the primary initiators and executioners of apoptosis.

questions.q: In the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway of apoptosis, release of which protein from the mitochondrial intermembrane space into the cytosol triggers apoptosome assembly and caspase-9 activation?
questions.explain: When pro-apoptotic BAX and BAK oligomerize in the outer mitochondrial membrane, cytochrome c leaks into the cytosol and binds Apaf-1 to form the apoptosome, activating initiator caspase-9.

open.q: Name the mitochondrial intermembrane protein whose release into the cytosol binds Apaf-1 to trigger apoptosome formation during intrinsic apoptosis.

questions.q: Which anti-apoptotic protein resides in the outer mitochondrial membrane and prevents apoptosis by inhibiting BAX and BAK oligomerization?
questions.explain: BCL-2 (along with BCL-XL and MCL-1) maintains outer mitochondrial membrane integrity by sequestering pro-apoptotic BH3-only sensors and preventing BAX/BAK channel formation.

open.q: Name the prototype anti-apoptotic protein located on the outer mitochondrial membrane that prevents cytochrome c release.

questions.q: Why does apoptosis fail to elicit an acute neutrophilic inflammatory reaction in surrounding tissues, unlike necrosis?
options: Apoptotic cells immediately neutralize all tissue complement proteins
Plasma membrane integrity is maintained and apoptotic bodies are rapidly phagocytosed
Apoptosis occurs exclusively in avascular epithelial tissues
Caspases digest all pro-inflammatory cytokines before cell division
questions.explain: During apoptosis, the plasma membrane remains intact but flips phosphatidylserine to its outer leaflet, serving as an eat-me signal for macrophages so apoptotic bodies are cleared before intracellular contents can leak out.

open.q: Why does apoptosis fail to trigger an acute inflammatory reaction in surrounding tissues compared with necrosis?

questions.q: Which phospholipid flips from the inner leaflet to the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane during apoptosis to serve as an eat-me signal for macrophages?
questions.explain: Phosphatidylserine is normally restricted to the inner leaflet by flippases; during apoptosis, scramblases expose it on the outer surface where macrophage receptors recognize it for silent clearance.

open.q: Name the plasma membrane phospholipid that flips to the outer leaflet during apoptosis to mark the cell for macrophage phagocytosis.

questions.q: Which form of programmed necrosis is triggered by TNF receptor signaling when caspase-8 is inhibited and depends on the kinase activity of RIPK1 and RIPK3?
questions.explain: Necroptosis morphologically resembles necrosis (cell swelling, membrane rupture, inflammation) but is genetically regulated through RIPK1, RIPK3, and MLKL phosphorylation when caspase-8 is blocked.

open.q: Name the caspase-independent form of regulated necrosis mediated by RIPK1, RIPK3, and MLKL signaling.

questions.q: Which inflammasome-mediated form of regulated cell death involves caspase-1 activation, gasdermin D pore formation, and release of active interleukin-1 beta?
questions.explain: Pyroptosis occurs mainly in infected macrophages and dendritic cells upon inflammasome activation of caspase-1 (or caspase-4/5), cleaving gasdermin D to form membrane pores and releasing fever-inducing IL-1 beta.

open.q: Name the inflammasome- and caspase-1-dependent form of inflammatory cell death characterized by gasdermin D membrane pores and IL-1 beta release.

questions.q: In developed countries and increasingly in urban Nigeria, what is the most common cause of hepatic steatosis (fatty liver)?
options: Alcohol abuse and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease
questions.explain: Excessive alcohol intake and obesity/type 2 diabetes (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease) are the leading causes of abnormal triglyceride accumulation within hepatocytes.

open.q: What are the two most common clinical causes of hepatic steatosis (fatty change of the liver)?

questions.q: Which histochemical stain is routinely used on frozen tissue sections to confirm that clear cytoplasmic vacuoles represent neutral triglycerides rather than water or glycogen?
questions.explain: Routine paraffin processing dissolves lipids, leaving empty vacuoles; Oil Red O or Sudan IV stains neutral fat orange-red on frozen sections. Prussian blue stains iron and Congo red stains amyloid.

open.q: Name a histochemical stain used on frozen tissue sections to confirm intracellular neutral lipid accumulation.

questions.q: Intracellular eosinophilic hyaline inclusions composed of damaged keratin intermediate filaments within hepatocytes in alcoholic hepatitis are known as what?
questions.explain: Mallory-Denk bodies are tangled skeins of ubiquitinated keratin intermediate filaments seen in hepatocytes in alcoholic steatohepatitis and metabolic steatohepatitis. Russell bodies are immunoglobulin inclusions in plasma cells.

open.q: Name the eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions of damaged keratin filaments found in hepatocytes in alcoholic hepatitis.

questions.q: Which histochemical stain reacts with ferric iron in haemosiderin granules to produce an intense blue colour?
questions.explain: In the Perls Prussian blue reaction, potassium ferrocyanide reacts with ferric iron (Fe3+) in tissue haemosiderin to form insoluble ferric ferrocyanide (Prussian blue).

open.q: Name the histochemical stain used to identify haemosiderin by turning ferric iron deposits bright blue.

questions.q: Dystrophic calcification differs from metastatic calcification because dystrophic calcification occurs under which condition?
options: In normal tissues in patients with hypercalcaemia
In necrotic or damaged tissues despite normal serum calcium levels
Exclusively within renal tubular epithelial cells
Only in patients with primary hyperparathyroidism
questions.explain: Dystrophic calcification is the deposition of calcium salts in dying or necrotic tissues (such as atheromatous plaques, damaged heart valves, and caseous tubercles) in patients with normal serum calcium and normal calcium metabolism.

open.q: How does dystrophic calcification differ from metastatic calcification regarding tissue status and serum calcium concentration?
accept: Occurs in necrotic tissue with normal serum calcium
Occurs in damaged tissue with normocalcaemia

questions.q: A 61-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease and secondary hyperparathyroidism develops widespread calcium deposits within the alveolar septa of her lungs and gastric mucosa. Which type of calcification is this?
questions.explain: Metastatic calcification affects previously normal tissues throughout the body (especially interstitial tissues of blood vessels, kidneys, lungs, and gastric mucosa) secondary to hypercalcaemia from causes like hyperparathyroidism, renal failure, or osteolytic tumours.

open.q: Name the type of pathologic calcification that occurs in normal tissues as a result of systemic hypercalcaemia.

questions.q: Progressive shortening of which specialized repetitive DNA sequences at the ends of linear chromosomes limits the replicative capacity of somatic cells and drives replicative senescence?
questions.explain: Telomeres (TTAGGG repeats) cap chromosome ends; because somatic cells lack telomerase, each cell division shortens telomeres until uncapped ends trigger a p53-mediated DNA damage response and permanent cell cycle arrest (replicative senescence).

open.q: Name the repetitive DNA sequences at chromosome ends whose progressive shortening drives replicative cellular senescence.
